title: The DEA is Trying to Blow Up Telemedicine for the Most Vulnerable
subtitle: Drastic restrictions on prescription of controlled substances is
body_html:
Welcome to The Frontier Psychiatrist newsletter. It's been a while since Telehealth prescribing of controlled substances was a topic of coverage here! Since the indictment of the founders of Done, it would've been tempting to think of the status quo had reached an uneasy detente.

It hasn’t. The DEA and HHS have been having some…disagreements…

Internal disagreement among HHS, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the White House budget office over the highly anticipated special registration system allowing for telehealth prescribing of controlled substances is delaying the second attempt at the proposed rule, three key industry lobbyists told Inside Health Policy Wednesday (Aug. 27) night.

To remind my readers—controlled substance prescribing historically required an in-person visit thanks to something called the Ryan Haight Act, which was intended to prevent online pill mills. When it was suspended, predictably, we got some online pill mills.

The pandemic waiver of in-person requirements allowing telehealth prescribing of controlled substances expires at the end of the calendar year, along with a myriad of other telehealth provisions. DEA is not interested in extending the pandemic-era flexibilities past the end of this calendar year and its draft rule undergoing White House review may be more restrictive than current flexibilities.

Keep in mind, some of the substances that are now being prescribed routinely include Suboxone for opiate use disorder. You know, the life-saving drug that prevent you from dying from overdose? Additionally, treatment for ADHD with stimulant medication has been in the crosshairs, and the prescribing of oral ketamine has become widespread. These things have not gone well. However, the restrictions being proposed by the DEA are even more severe than prior to the pandemic…

“It's game over, one way or the other,” the lobbyist said. “It almost wouldn't matter the [whether] the waiver elapses. If these are the rules that they want to move forward with, they would both effectively equally stop in its tracks . . . continued ability to prescribe these controlled substances for the most sensitive communities.”

How restrictive? Absurdly restrictive. I'm a psychiatrist, and I'm never gonna prescribe controlled substances by telehealth if the following is the regulation:

Supposedly in the proposed rule pending at the White House, to prescribe Schedule II-IV drugs, which include those used to treat ADHD, providers would have to search all 50 state Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) records before they remotely prescribe a controlled substance, which would effectively stop any use of the proposed special registration process, according to a lobbyist.

Many physicians moved their practice to entirely virtual over the course of the pandemic, and there are of course entire companies dedicated to servicing patients through telemedicine. Except, for the most vulnerable patients who require controlled substances to manage their conditions, not anymore:

The proposed rule may limit physicians to prescribing no more than 50% of their total prescriptions remotely, effectively eliminating remote-only, virtual-only providers, according to the lobbyist.

For many years, the DEA has delayed providing Congress with the proposed rule that they were mandated to do when Ryan Haight was introduced. That law specified the DEA crafting a special regulation for telehealth prescribing controlled substances. What the proposed regulations do is the opposite: rolling back the clock, and pulling back life-saving care from millions of people— overnight. We don't have a system capable of doing what we should be doing (according to reported DEA proposals), we don't have funding or systems to make that plausible, and people will die if the restrictions on telehealth prescription as above become law.

I respect my colleagues at DEA, I respect their purview, and I respect the need for appropriate enforcement. Creating unrealistic and wildly burdensome prescribing restrictions won't solve the problem of reducing risk from the substances, it will increase diversion.

Responsible physicians need to know how to be responsible in a way that allows them to take care of their patients, not in a way that requires them to check 50 separate state registries every time they want to write a single prescription.

Readers, makes some noise…

Share
